_comment: Legendary and hagiographic narratives cut from the Russian Primary Chronicle (Laurentian text), trans. S. H. Cross & O. P. Sherbowitz-Wetzor (1930, public domain as of 2026). All passages paraphrase.

title.en: The Calling of the Varangians: 'Our Land Is Great and Rich, but There Is No Order'
title.zh: 瓦良格人之召請：『我土廣而富，獨無秩序』

region.zh: 諾夫哥羅德（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event dated 862; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text, trans. S. H. Cross and O. P. Sherbowitz-Wetzor (1930), s.a. 862

summary.en: The founding scene of Russian history: after expelling the Varangians who taxed them, the tribes fall to feuding; they send over the sea to the Rus, saying 'Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come to rule and reign over us' — and three brothers answer.
summary.zh: 俄羅斯史之開篇：驅走徵貢之瓦良格人後，諸部內亂不已；遂遣使渡海赴羅斯，曰『我土廣而富，獨無秩序。請來君臨而治之』——兄弟三人應召而至。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle founding legend; contested by modern historians (Normanist debate) — flagged in note.

passages.text: The tributaries of the Varangians drove them back beyond the sea and, refusing them further tribute, set out to govern themselves. There was no law among them, but tribe rose against tribe: quarrelling among themselves, they began to war one with another. They said to themselves, 'Let us seek a prince who may rule over us and judge according to the Law.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 862 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: They accordingly went overseas to the Varangian Rus: these particular Varangians were known as Rus, as some are known as Swedes and others as Norwegians. The Chuds, the Slavs, the Krivichians, and the Ves then said to the people of Rus, 'Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come to rule and reign over us.' Thus three brothers, with their kinfolk, took with them all the Rus and came — and the eldest, Rurik, settled in Novgorod: the city that would name the dynasty of Russia for seven hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 862 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Oleg and the Death of His Horse: The Skull of the Serpent
title.zh: 奧列格與愛馬之死：馬頭骨下之蛇

region.en: Kiev, mound by the Dnieper (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔第聶伯河畔古塚（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event dated 912; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 912

summary.en: Magi foretold Prince Oleg that the horse he rode would be his death; he had it kept and fed, never to be mounted, and five years later, the horse dead and its bones white, he laughed at the prophecy over the skull — and the serpent that glided from it stung his foot, fulfilling the word of the wise men.
summary.zh: 巫師預言奧列格王公：其坐騎將致其死；遂令人飼馬而不乘。五年後馬死骨白，王公臨馬頭骨笑其妄——骨中滑出之蛇嚙其足，巫言乃驗。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; parallel to the death-foretelling horse of many traditions.

passages.text: Prince Oleg asked his wise men and magi what his death would be, and they answered that the horse he loved and rode would be the cause of his death. He took thought then, and commanded that the horse should not be brought before him again; he ordered it kept and fed apart, never to be mounted, and after some years had it led away. He wept for the beast he had ridden so long, and rebuked the magi, saying their words were false.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 912 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Five years after the death of his horse Oleg asked where its bones were, and learning they were still on the spot, he laughed at the prophecy: 'Are these my death?' He set his foot upon the skull; but a serpent glided out from it and stung him in the foot, so that he sickened and died — and all the people mourned him greatly. His tomb remains by legend to this day, and it is known as Oleg's Grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 912 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Igor: A Prince Greedy for Tribute
title.zh: 伊戈爾之死：貢斂過甚之王公

region.en: Iskorosten, land of the Drevlians (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 德列夫利安人之伊斯科羅斯堅（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

texts.period: Event dated 945; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: After collecting the tribute, Igor went back for more; the Drevlians said 'If a wolf comes among the sheep, he will carry off the whole flock' — and rising against the prince who returned with a small escort, they killed him and buried him beneath a felled tree.
summary.zh: 伊戈爾收貢之後復往求貢；德列夫利人云『狼入羊群，則盡驅其群』——遂起而殺此僅率少從復來之王公，斬樹覆其尸而葬之。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle narrative; the wolf-proverb became a Russian byword for predatory rule.

passages.text: After his campaign Igor had gone about the land of the Drevlians collecting tribute, and had added it to the former exactions. Returning to Kiev he sent to the people of Iskorosten, demanding a further tribute. On the advice of his retinue — Sweneld's men, who had gathered much wealth — Igor himself went back for more, with a small company, coveting the great sum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Drevlians, hearing of his approach, took counsel with their prince Mal: 'If a wolf comes among the sheep, he will carry off the whole flock, unless he be killed; so will it be with us, if we do not slay Igor — he will destroy us all.' Taking weapons they went forth against Igor and his few followers and killed him; the chronicle says they buried him beneath a felled tree. So died the prince whose oath on Perun's hill the year before had sworn his descendants into slavery if they broke faith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Olga's First Revenge: The Envoy in the Boat-Pit
title.zh: 奧爾加的第一復仇：舟坑葬使

region.en: Kiev and the Drevlian land (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 基輔與德列夫利安之地（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

texts.period: Event dated 945-946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: When the Drevlians proposed that Olga marry their prince Mal, she had their first embassy carried in state — then tipped into a trench and buried alive; to their second she offered a bath of honour, and locked the door.
summary.zh: 德列夫利人提議奧爾加嫁其王公馬爾；她先禮遇第一批使節——隨即掀翻獨木舟、活埋於坑；再請第二批入浴室沐浴榮寵——而閉其門。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; Olga's fourfold revenge became a classic of Russian storytelling and Orthodox sainthood.

passages.text: When the Drevlians heard that Igor was dead they sent twenty of their best men to Olga, proposing that she take their prince Mal for her husband. Olga answered graciously that her husband's death was a thing she could not forget, but that on the morrow she would do them honour before her people. She bade a great boat be brought, and the Drevlians sat in it, proudly, clad in their finest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Olga commanded a deep pit to be dug in the courtyard. The boat with the envoys was carried out, cast into the trench with the men still sitting in their splendour; and bending over them she asked: 'Is it to your taste?' — and ordered them buried alive. So the first embassy of the Drevlians went the way they had prepared for others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Olga's Second Revenge: The Bath of Honour
title.zh: 奧爾加的第二復仇：榮寵之浴

texts.period: Event dated 945-946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: The Drevlians sent their best men for a second wooing; Olga offered them the honour of a bath before an audience with the Princess — and the bathhouse door was barred behind them, the fire kindled beneath, so that all were steamed to death.
summary.zh: 德列夫利人再遣其最優之使求婚；奧爾加許以入浴之榮——浴堂之門閉而火起於下，眾使盡斃於蒸氣之中。

passages.text: Olga then sent to the Drevlians: 'If you ask me in truth, send your best men to my city, that I may go to your prince with great honour.' The Drevlians chose their most distinguished men and sent them. On their arrival Olga offered water for the bath, saying: 'Wash yourselves and appear before me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bathhouse was heated, and the Drevlians entered in to wash; Olga ordered the door secured behind them and fire set to it from the windows, so that all were burned to death together. Then she sent a message to Iskorosten: 'I have received your first envoys, and now prepare a great feast for your best men, that I may mourn over the grave of my husband and hold a funeral feast for him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Olga's Third Revenge: The Funeral Feast of Iskorosten
title.zh: 奧爾加的第三復仇：伊斯科羅斯堅之喪宴

region.en: Grave of Igor at Iskorosten (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 伊斯科羅斯堅伊戈爾之墓（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

texts.period: Event dated 946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 945

summary.en: At Igor's grave mound Olga bade the Drevlians drink to the stricken prince; when they were drunk she asked her followers to fall upon them — and five thousand died in the single night, so that she went home to raise an army against the rest.
summary.zh: 於伊戈爾塚前，奧爾加命德列夫利人為其『苦主』王公飲酒；眾醉之際，她命扈從掩殺——一夜之間五千人殞命；歸而點兵，以討其餘。

passages.text: Olga went with a small retinue to the grave of Igor at Iskorosten and wept over her husband. Then she commanded her followers to pile a great mound, and when it was done ordered a funeral feast. When the Drevlians had drunk heavily she said to her followers, 'Now fall upon them' — and they cut down the Drevlians, and about five thousand of them perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Olga returned to Kiev and mustered an army against the remnant; the next year she marched with her son Svyatoslav into the Drevlian land. The city held against her the first summer; then, by her devices, the city was taken and burned — the fourth and greatest of her revenges, which the chronicle tells next with the pigeons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Olga's Fourth Revenge: Doves and Sparrows with Burning Tow
title.zh: 奧爾加的第四復仇：縛炬之鴿雀

region.en: Iskorosten, Drevlian land (symbolic pin at Korosten)
region.zh: 德列夫利安之伊斯科羅斯堅（象徵性定位於科羅斯堅）

texts.period: Event dated 946; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 946

summary.en: The city offered three pigeons and three sparrows from every house as tribute; Olga bade each bird carry a burning match tied behind — and when they flew home to their nests, no house remained standing in the city that had killed her husband.
summary.zh: 城中按戶獻鴿雀各三隻為貢；奧爾加命每鳥縛燃火細芒於其後——鳥各飛歸其巢，殺其夫之城遂無一屋立於火後。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; the trick is paralleled in Chinese, Norse, and Indian siege tales.

passages.text: Iskorosten stood firm behind its walls, and Olga encamped before the city the whole summer. Then she sent this message: 'What do you want of me? I have taken vengeance on your princes and your city — I do not desire tribute to levy it again; I asked it once. Pay me the tribute, and I will depart.' The Drevlians asked what she wanted, and Olga answered, 'Give me three pigeons and three sparrows from each house.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 946 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: The citizens rejoiced and gathered the birds. Olga gave her soldiers a command, saying to each: 'Tie a match to each pigeon and sparrow, with a small piece of cloth wrapped in sulphur and bound with thread.' When darkness fell she released the birds, and each flew to its own nest — to the pigeon-coops, the pigeon-perches, and the eaves — and so the dove-cotes, the roofs, the porches, and the hayricks caught fire, and there was not a house that was not consumed, so that all fled in flight from the city. The people who escaped were taken prisoner, the city burned, the first citizens slain, others made to pay tribute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 946 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Olga in Constantinople: Baptism and the Wily Emperor
title.zh: 奧爾加在君士坦丁堡：受洗與狡黠皇帝

region.zh: 君士坦丁堡聖索菲亞（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event dated 955 (or 957); recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 955

summary.en: Olga, regent of Russia, journeyed to Constantinople and was baptized Helena by the Patriarch; the Emperor Constantine, delighted by her beauty and wisdom, offered to make her his daughter — and she answered that she was his goddaughter and could not marry her own godfather, so he laughed and sent her home with gifts.
summary.zh: 俄羅斯攝政奧爾加赴君士坦丁堡，受洗名海倫娜；康斯坦丁帝慕其美貌才智，欲娶之為后——她答：我是您的教女，教父怎能娶教女？帝大笑而厚禮遣歸。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle-hagiographic account; historical details contested (baptism date, 'daughters' pun).

passages.text: Olga, regent for her son Svyatoslav, went to Constantinople with many gifts and arrived at the city of the Greek Emperor. The Emperor Constantine saw her and was struck by her beauty and her wisdom; he conversed with her and perceived that she was wise beyond all others. He said to her, 'You are worthy to reign in this city with me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 955 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: She was instructed in the faith and baptized by the Patriarch Polyeuktos, who named her Helena — after the mother of Constantine the Great. The Emperor said to her, 'I wish to take you as my wife.' She answered: 'How can you marry me, after yourself baptizing me and calling me your daughter? For among Christians that is not lawful. You know it yourself.' Then the Emperor said, 'You have outwitted me, Olga' — and gave her many gifts and dismissed her in peace, calling her his daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 955 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: She returned to Kiev with priests and Christian books, and tried to convert her son Svyatoslav, who laughed and would not follow; but the chronicle makes her the dawn of Russian Christianity — 'Olga was the forerunner of the Christian land, even as the day-spring precedes the sun, and as the moon precedes the day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 955 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: The Faiths on Trial: Vladimir's Debate of 986
title.zh: 信仰的法庭：九八六年弗拉基米爾辯道

texts.period: Event dated 986; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 986

summary.en: Missionaries of four faiths came to Vladimir's hall — Volga Bulgars with one god and circumcision, Germans of the Pope, Khazar Jews of Abraham's wandering god, and a Greek philosopher with an icon of the Last Judgment; he dismissed the rest with 'Drinking is the joy of the Russes; we cannot exist without that pleasure' and kept only the Greek.
summary.zh: 四教使節至弗拉基米爾之殿——伏爾加保加利亞人（割禮一神）、教皇之德意志人、可薩猶太人（亞伯拉罕流離之神）、以及持末世審判像之希臘哲士；他遣走前者，言『飲酒乃羅斯人之樂，離之不能活』，獨留希臘哲士。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle polemic; the debate is a literary construction of Christian historiography, flagged in note.

passages.text: The Bulgars of Mohammedan faith came first, saying that though Vladimir was a wise and prudent prince, he had no religion: adopt theirs and believe in their god, who loved circumcision, eating no pork, no wine, and promising after death pleasures — every man seventy wives in paradise. Vladimir asked what their land's other delight was, and they answered no other delight; he found their law distasteful and answered that 'Drinking is the joy of the Russes. We cannot exist without that pleasure.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 986 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came Germans from the Pope of Rome and Khazar Jews who told how their god Abraham had cast out the many nations of the land; Vladimir dismissed both — the Germans because their faith was but a Latin shadow of the Greek, the Jews asking 'Where is your land?' 'In Jerusalem.' 'God is angry with our fathers and scattered us for our sins; our land was given to the Christians.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 986 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Last came a philosopher from the Greeks, who told Vladimir of the world from Adam to the Flood, and then spoke of the world to come. He showed him a curtain painted with the Last Judgment: the angels on the right and the sinners on the left, in torment. 'Glad are those on the right hand, but wretched those on the left.' Vladimir sighed and said, 'Good for them on the right; woe to those on the left.' He inclined his heart to Christianity, and having seen this vision, he delayed only until the wise men of his retinue could test the faith in the lands that kept it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 986-987 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Vladimir at Korsun: Blindness Healed in the Baptismal Font
title.zh: 弗拉基米爾在科爾松：洗禮池中復明

region.zh: 克里米亞科爾松（赫爾松涅斯）（象徵性定位於塞瓦斯托波爾）

texts.period: Event dated 988; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 988

summary.en: Vladimir besieged Korsun and demanded the emperor's sister Anna; blind, he was baptized in the church of St. Basil at her urging — and opening his eyes, cried 'I have now beheld the true God!' He gave the city back to the Greeks, married Anna, and carried home the faith.
summary.zh: 弗拉基米爾圍科爾松，求帝妹安娜為妻；雙目失明，安娜勸其受洗——於聖巴西爾堂洗禮之際睜眼呼曰：『我今見真神矣！』歸城於希臘人，娶安娜，携信仰而返。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend of conversion; historical reality was more gradual.

passages.text: Vladimir marched on Korsun, the Greek city in the Crimea, and besieged it. From the ramparts a citizen named Anastasius shot arrows with messages, telling how the wells from which the city drank its water lay behind; Vladimir stopped the springs and the city thirsted into surrender. He sent word to Byzantium that he desired to marry the Emperor's sister Anna, threatening otherwise to do to Constantinople what he had done to Korsun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 988 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anna came weeping across the water, saying she was going as if to captivity; but when Vladimir, who had suffered an illness of the eyes and was quite blind, heard her say that if he were baptized he would regain his sight, he answered, 'If this alone be true, then truly is the God of the Christians great' — and was baptized in the church of St. Basil. When the priest laid his hand upon him, Vladimir opened his eyes and saw: 'I have now beheld the true God!' Astounded at the miracle, Anna and all who saw gave glory to God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 988 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: He gave Korsun back to the Greeks as dowry for his bride, married Anna in the same church, and returned to Kiev with the princess, priests, and relics of St. Clement. There he baptized his twelve sons in the Dnieper, then ordered the idols overthrown and the whole city baptized in the river, princes and slaves alike standing in the water while the priests read the baptismal prayer — and heaven rejoiced over so many souls saved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 988 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Boris and Gleb: The Princes Who Would Not Fight
title.zh: 鮑里斯與格列布：不肯相爭的兩位王公

region.zh: 阿爾塔河與斯摩棱斯克（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Events dated 1015; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 1015

summary.en: When Vladimir died, Svyatopolk seized Kiev and sent men to kill his half-brothers: Boris prayed on the riverbank as the assassins came and offered his throat; Gleb, still a boy in his boat on the river, was told his father wished to see him — and submitted, meek as a lamb, to the stroke.
summary.zh: 弗拉基米爾薨，斯維亞托波爾克據基輔遣人殺其異母弟：鮑里斯於河畔禱告，遇刺客至而引頸就戮；格列布尚在舟中，聞『父欲見汝』——如羔羊般順服受刃。

sensitivity.note: Hagiographic narrative; first native saints of Russia; political reading (Svyatopolk's guilt) is debated.

passages.text: Vladimir died at Berestovo, and Svyatopolk seized the throne at Kiev and killed his brother's men. Boris was marching home with his army when messengers told him of his father's death and offered him the throne — his men were many and Svyatopolk's were not. Boris answered that he could not lift his hand against his elder brother: 'It is not for me to rise against my elder brother; for if my father be dead, this man shall stand in my father's place.' His soldiers left him, and he stood alone on the river Alta with his household servants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1015 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Svyatopolk's assassins came at night; Boris sang the psalms and prayed, knowing that they were coming to kill him. He looked upon them and they came in — his servant George, a Hungarian, was slain defending him. Then they pierced Boris with lances and spears. Still breathing, he was carried to Svyatopolk's men, who ended him in his tent; so the prince died offering no resistance, and was mourned by all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1015 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Gleb, sailing down the Dnieper, was met by Svyatopolk's messengers, who said his father wished to see him — for he was sick. Gleb landed and went along the bank; then they seized him, and their leader, like a second Cain, bade the cook kill the lamb of God. Gleb prayed aloud: 'Do not this deed, my brothers, do not this deed! What have I done to you? If my brother has done wickedness, am I also his brother? But do not take my life — a lamb in innocence stands amid the shearers.' He was killed in his boat, near Smolensk, and was mourned as one 'meek as a lamb'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1015 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Yaroslav the Wise: Books like Rivers Watering the Earth
title.zh: 智者雅羅斯拉夫：書如江河潤澤大地

region.en: Kiev, church of St. Sophia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔聖索菲亞堂（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event dated 1037; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 1037

summary.en: Yaroslav loved books and assembled scribes to translate Greek volumes into Slavonic: 'Great is the benefit from book-learning; for books are like rivers that water the whole earth — they are the springs of wisdom, and have in themselves an immeasurable depth.'
summary.zh: 雅羅斯拉夫愛書，聚書手譯希臘典籍為斯拉夫文：『書學之益大矣；書如江河，潤澤大地——乃智慧之泉，其中蘊藏不可測之深。』

passages.text: Yaroslav loved books and religion, and was zealous for churches and for the Christian law. He gathered many scribes and set them to translate from Greek into Slavonic; and they wrote and collected many books by which true believers are instructed and enjoy religious education.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1037 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: As one land is ploughed by many, so Yaroslav — in the chronicler's figure — sowed the written words of the law in the hearts of believers: 'Great is the benefit from book-learning; for by books we are taught and instructed in the way of repentance, and gain wisdom and continence. For books are like rivers that water the whole earth; they are the springs of wisdom, and books have in themselves an immeasurable depth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1037 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Vladimir Monomakh's Testament: 'Do Not Let the Powerful Destroy the Weak'
title.zh: 莫諾馬赫遺訓：『勿令強者害弱者』

texts.period: Composed c. 1101-1117, appended to the Laurentian text; Cross trans. 1930

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), Appendix I: The Testament of Vladimir Monomakh

summary.en: The dying prince's letter to his children mixes psalm and proverb, battle and prayer: do not let the powerful destroy any — Christian or poor — nor the powerful eat the weak; give to the orphan, defend the widow, and never swerve from the oath sworn on the cross.
summary.zh: 垂死王公致其子之書，雜以詩篇、箴言、征戰與祈禱：勿令強者加害於人——無論基督徒或貧者——勿令強者吞弱者；撫孤兒、護寡婦，十字架前所立之誓，不可偏離。

sensitivity.note: Autobiographical testament, a classic of Old Russian literature.

passages.text: Vladimir Monomakh, prince of Kiev, wrote his children a testament seated in thought upon his sledge — an old man thinking on death. He tells them first what his father taught him, then sets down the lessons of his life: 'Have pride of soul in your hearts and minds, but think no pride of body, for all is mortal — the flower withers, the smoke disperses, the vapor scatters away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Testament of Vladimir Monomakh in the Primary Chronicle, Appendix I (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Above all things, do not forget the poor, and support them and give to the orphan as far as you are able, and defend the widow yourselves, and do not let the powerful destroy any man. Kill neither right nor wrong, nor order any to be slain, even though he be unworthy of death. Do not let the powerful destroy any — Christian or otherwise.' His own account of his campaigns — hunting, riding, war, and councils from morning till night — stands as a prince's rule of work: never idle, never drunken, never prideful, and above all never forsworn of the oath made at the cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Testament of Vladimir Monomakh (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

title.en: Portents of 1065: The Eclipse and the Frankish Comets
title.zh: 一〇六五年之異象：日蝕與法蘭克彗星

region.en: Kievan Rus, sky over the Dnieper (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔羅斯第聶伯上空（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Events dated 1065; recorded in the Primary Chronicle (Cross trans. 1930)

source.work: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text (1930), s.a. 1065

summary.en: In the year 1065 the sun was eclipsed — 'there was great sorrow over the Russian land, in consequence of the eclipse which God sent upon us'; a star of blood appeared over the church of the Holy Wisdom, and the chronicler links the sign to the princes' fatal quarrels.
summary.zh: 一〇六五年日有蝕——『俄羅斯大地因此神所降之蝕而大悲』；血色之星現於聖智堂上空，史家以此兆繫於王公們致命之內爭。

passages.text: In the year 1065 the sun was eclipsed, and there was great sorrow over the Russian land in consequence of the eclipse which God sent upon us. A star in the west portended bloodshed; the sign was seen from the sky, like a dragon in the heavens, and the chronicler counts the calamities that followed — death among princes, battle, and famine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1065 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.

passages.text: Portents in the chronicle are theology, not astronomy: God sends signs so that men may turn from evil deeds. The stars fall, the earth quakes, children speak words, and each marvel is set beside the sins that invited it. In the Old Russian cosmology the sky reads like scripture — and every eclipse is a parenthesis in a sentence about justice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Primary Chronicle, s.a. 1065 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1930); not verbatim.
